subsubtopic: DEMAND THAT GOVERNMENT ACT TO REDUCE INTEREST RATES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Liberal government's high interest rate policy, designed to reduce inflation, is not working. In fact it is inducing inflation as well as being the main cause of hundreds of bankruptcies and the loss of homes and farms. Industries and businesses are closing down, and more than a million people are looking for jobs. In fact high interest is largely the cause of the present Liberal depression, but still the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) refuse stubbornly to bite the bullet. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro):
That this House demands that the government take action immediately or resign.
Hon. members on this side of the Chamber will not sit on the sidelines much longer and see this country go to wrack and ruin.

ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY POLITICAL PARTIES SASKATCHEWAN GOVERNMENT POLICIES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the unemployment figures released today show that, despite our country's wealth and resources, officially over 9 per cent of our labour force cannot find work. Yet Saskatchewan, which just a few years ago was a have-not province, has now the lowest unemployment rate in Canada. Through sound management of its resources and the economy, the government of Allan Blakeney has provided economic stability, steady growth, and a balanced budget, at a time when the rest of the country is experiencing an economic depression. Saskatchewan has led the way in pioneering new social programs and is now a leader in economic planning and management. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse):
That the House recognize the success of the Saskatchewan government under Allan Blakeney in managing its economy and that the Government of Canada follow the lead Saskatchewan has provided.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER WITHDRAW OR AMEND BUDGET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. I know he will be aware from the statistics this morning that the unemployment rate now stands at 9 per cent. That is the highest level of unemployment the country has suffered since we started keeping monthly records, indeed the highest level since World War II. Also the minister knows that all but one of the major economic indicators indicate a decline, and I am sure he was not surprised to learn from the statistics this morning that there are 166,000 fewer people working this year than last year.
We all know that the minister has been consulting with economic leaders across the country and these statistics ought not to be a surprise to him. In light of this disastrous economic news, will the minister advise the House whether he intends either to withdraw his budget or bring in substantial amendments to it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER WITHDRAW OR AMEND BUDGET
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am aware of the unemployment statistics which are very serious indeed. The hon. member suggested that I consider withdrawing the budget. I wonder whether he is including in that question the thought that I should withdraw from the current monetary and fiscal policy which is being followed by the Government of Canada.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER WITHDRAW OR AMEND BUDGET
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER WITHDRAW OR AMEND BUDGET
speechtext: If that is his proposal, then I think I should like to hear it from him directly.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, of course my question was a simple one. I just asked the minister whether he would either withdraw his budget or change it. In the absence of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, perhaps I should direct my supplementary question to his parliamentary secretary, his acting minister, or to the Minister of Finance. Indeed, it is a specific question; perhaps the Minister of Finance can help.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: I will try.

A year ago the Industrial and Labour Adjustment Program was established to deal with those areas of the country which were hardest hit. The program itself has been characterized more by public relations announcements from

the minister than any activity on the street. I have three specific questions. How many jobs have been created by that program in Sydney, Cape Breton Island, where the unemployment rate is 22.4 per cent? How many jobs have been created in the Eastern Townships where the unemployment rate is 18.2 per cent? How many jobs have been created in McAdam, New Brunswick, where the unemployment rate is 15.1 per cent? All three of those regions have applied. I should like the minister, or whomever he can call on, to tell those people and me how many actual jobs have been created.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad the hon. member referred to the Industrial Labour Adjustment Program under which the Government of Canada allocated $350 million to help industry and labour to adjust more effectively to current economic circumstances. Unfortunately I do not have the specific projects for each of the designated areas.
I know, for example, that the industrial adjustment committee in Sydney, Nova Scotia, has been working diligently, and so valuable did it think the program that it requested that labour benefits be extended to the longshoremen of North Sydney and Newfoundland. This past week the cabinet decided to extend the benefits to these affected workers. That is one evidence for the hon. member to appreciate that the program is working effectively. Also I know, for example, that quite a number of members, who represent areas with difficult economic circumstances, have asked that the benefits of the program be extended to their communities. We have been designating communities, as justified, in order to take advantage of this very important program.

subsubtopic: MR. McKINNON-ALTERATIONS TO REMARKS OF MR. LAMONTAGNE IN COMMITTEE MEETING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. You may recall that a few days ago I attempted to raise a question of privilege concerning the report which has just been tabled and the evidence given supporting that report. I was somewhat encouraged when, in reply to my House leader, the House leader of the official opposition, on March 22 Your Honour said:
The hon. member is quite right. If at a later time this grievance is reported to the House, then it can be discussed in the House.
The report is now in front of the House, and my understanding is that now is the time when I should present my question of privilege, a summation of which I sent to Your Honour on March 22. This question of privilege concerns the altering of minutes of a meeting of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
I draw to Your Honour's attention the Nineteenth Edition of Eskine May at page 141, where it states:
It is a breach of privilege to present or cause to be presented to either House or to committees of either House forged, falsified or fabricated documents with intent to deceive such House or committees or to subscribe the names of other persons or fictitious names to documents intended to be presented to either House or committees of either House, or to be privy to, or cognizant of, such forgery or fraud.
Further on, and perhaps more closely related to this point, Erskine May says:
-to falsify or improperly alter any records of, or documents presented to, either House or committees of either House will constitute a contempt. Standing Order No. 78 of the House of Commons specifically provides that no document received by the clerk of a select committee shall be withdrawn or altered without the knowledge and approval of the committee.
When giving evidence before the committee on February 25, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) gave

April 8, 1982
Privilege-Mr. McKinnon
evidence, clearly heard and factually reported in the electronic transcript, which was altered before the minutes were printed.
The first offence, which was of a minor nature, was when the minister introduced two separate members of his staff as both being one Mr. W. M. Beckett, director of arms control policy. The other gentleman was in fact Mr. Mathewson, the chief of policy planning. This was, as I said, a minor alteration, although his chief of policy planning might consider it surprising that he is unknown to the minister. However, the minister went on with his unusual naming, showing a much more serious lack of knowledge of who's who.
At one page of the transcript the minister referred to a Mr. Khrushchev suggesting a disarmament policy; and, incidentally, he used the present tense. In the minutes of the meeting "Mr. Khrushchev" has been deleted and "Mr. Brezhnev" substituted. To indicate that this was no mistake, Mr. Khrushchev, who has been dead for ten years, makes three more miraculous visitations in the minister's testimony in the transcript, only to turn into Mr. Brezhnev in the minutes.
Madam Speaker, it is no minor matter when our Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) is unaware of who is in charge of the mightiest conventional forces in the world; but we are not here to judge the minister's acuity. A lack of acuity is not an offence under the rules of Parliament. Changing the records of a committee is, and the records of that committee were changed, without the permission of the committee.
The members of the committee have been apprised by the chairman of the committee of what happened. We are now informed that a Mr. MacKay, an assistant to the minister, who appears to have a job somewhat analogous to the man with a wheelbarrow and shovel who follows the elephant in a circus-parade-

Order, please. It took me some time to check into the notices that had been given to me to find out exactly what the hon. member was referring to. I have to point out to the hon. member that he is speaking of alterations to the minutes of a committee, which alterations, he is saying now, were discussed in the committee but not reported to the House.
At first I thought that perhaps the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) was referring to a report of the committee as tabled in the House, but as tabled in the House does not report on the alteration of the minutes of which the hon. member is now speaking. This question, therefore, obviously had to be dealt with within the committee. Since it is not before the House and has not been reported to the House, I am afraid I cannot deal with it.
The recourse which I think the hon. member followed, which was to bring up the question at the committee meeting, has been taken. I know he is not satisfied with the results of that recourse taken in committee, but I am afraid that since it is not before the House I cannot help the hon. member.

I was informed by Your Honour that I could not present this matter to the House until the report had been submitted to the House, which is the case now. If you rule that I have no question of privilege, I will accept your ruling and will consider that any member of a committee can change the records of that committee at any time without breaching the privilege of anyone.

What are the names and addresses of all Soviet news media personnel accredited to work in Canada by the Department of External Affairs and, in each case, which news agency does he/she represent?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Foreign news media representatives in Canada are not accredited by the Department of External Affairs. Accreditation of the individual as representing a particular publication or broadcasting organization is by his or her employer in the country of origin. Canadian recognition of the status of Soviet news media representatives resident in Canada is accorded by the granting of an appropriate visa by the Department of Employment and Immigration. In October, 1977, the Canadian and Soviet governments agreed, in accordance with the provisions of the Helsinki Final Act, that each country would grant to resident media representatives of the other country (and to members of their families) multiple entry-exit visas valid for one year. The validity of the visa is subject to extension.
At present, there are four Soviet news media representatives resident in Canada. They are: Mr. N. I. Bragin, representing Pravda; Mr. R. L. Kurkin, representing the Soviet State Committee for Radio and TV; Mr. A. O. Melikyan, representing Tass; and Mr. A. V. Sandakov, representing Novosti. As explained in answer to question No. 3,030 tabled this day, the department does not make public the private addresses of individuals without the express permission of the person concerned. All resident Soviet media representatives live in Ottawa, however, and can be reached through the press office of the Soviet Embassy.

Were there cases when Millhaven inmates were not attended by a proctor during the examination but where those appointed to act as such from the Millhaven staff absented themselves, while at the same time pocketing the fee for rendering such services, and, if so, what were all the details and the names of the persons involved?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In so far as the
Correctional Service of Canada is concerned:
1.	The educational program at Millhaven Institution is supplemented by correspondence programs from outside North American recognized educational agencies including the
Order Paper Questions
University of Waterloo, and all written examinations in these courses are supervised or proctored at all times.
2.	All written examinations pertaining to outside educational agencies are "proctored" or "supervised" by the Supervisor of Academic Education, Mr. C. W. Greaves.
3.	No examination to date has been unattended or unsupervised. The examinations are personally delivered to the inmate-candidate on the appointed date, time and place and in accordance with the instructions issued by the particular educational agency. Supervision is maintained throughout the examination and at the end of the three-hour writing or the surrendering of the paper by the candidate, whichever comes first, papers are collected, sealed and mailed to their destination.
With respect to fees for proctoring examinations, none of the educational agencies, with the exception of the University of Waterloo, pays any fees. The University of Waterloo pays $23 per half day for supervising examinations but most of its examinations must be written on a Saturday since the university requires its examinations be written sometime during the weekend (Friday evening to Monday morning) and be mailed first thing Monday morning. Mr. Greaves does not request overtime compensation or travel allowance for his proctoring attendance on such occasions. The examinations are mailed to his home.

speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its chronic failure to implement policies to support the development of a sound industrial sector for Canada, and for the resulting lay-off crisis in every sector of the economy and every region of the country, which has had particularly severe consequences for the auto industry, the resource industry, the energy projects and the producers of consumer goods and appliances.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in the debate today, particularly when the statistics published this morning by Statistics Canada indicate that we have an unemployment rate which is higher than it has been at any time in recent memory and, indeed, higher than it has been since soon after World War II.
An article in The Globe and Mail on April 7, 1982, which reported on an interview with Governor Gerald Bouey of the Bank of Canada as follows:
"I am sometimes asked how high does the rate of unemployment have to go, how many foreclosures have to occur, before the bank will give up its policy of monetary restraint," he told a Canadian Club audience of businessmen sprinkled with top civil servants.
Supply
"Since surrendering to inflation is no answer to our problem, one might better ask how long will it take Canadians to respond realistically, to take the financial discipline our situation requires-"
How long will it take Canadians to recognize the importance of financial discipline, Mr. Speaker? I do not know how Governor Bouey sees the world. He may see it differently if he is talking to people who make substantial sums of money and top civil servants who also make substantial sums of money. When he talks about telling Canadians that they should be more realistic and impose upon themselves a financial discipline, I am interested to know-and the report did not cover this-which Canadians he is talking about. Where do they live? Who are they?
Surely he cannot be referring to the 1,229,000 on record as being unemployed. They are obviously already exercising financial discipline. Perhaps he meant the three million Canadians who live below the Statistics Canada poverty line- that's 12 per cent of our population. I do not think he meant them either.
Nor do I think he meant the 42 per cent of high school graduates who are looking for work and cannot find it. They are obviously exercising some financial discipline.
Maybe he meant the part-time workers in Canada who need and are looking for full-time jobs and cannot find them. There are 45,000 of them in Toronto alone. Maybe he meant that they should exercise financial discipline.
Perhaps he is talking about the quarter of a million unemployed employables that the Assistant Deputy Minister of National Health and Welfare talked about two days ago. They are the "unemployed employables". I am sure he did not mean they should exercise financial discipline.
Maybe he meant the 500 people laid off yesterday by Eaton's in Toronto. Maybe he meant the 6,200 people laid off in the shoe industry. Perhaps he meant the 1,500 International Harvester workers who will be laid off by May. Perhaps he meant the third of the industrial work force in the automotive industry. Perhaps he meant that those people should be exercising financial discipline.
Perhaps he meant that the 600,000 senior citizens who are living below the Statistics Canada poverty line should be exercising financial discipline. Perhaps he meant the farmers in the country who will have 15 per cent less income. Who was he talking about? It cannot be all of those people; it cannot be any of those people.
The fact of the matter is that when it comes to the financial discipline index, people are joining in the thousands every day. They may not be the top public servants of whom he spoke the other day. It might be helpful to everyone if Governor Bouey, and those he serves on the government side, made clear from whom they want financial discipline. Why are all these people being forced, while others are not, into such financial discipline?

April 8, 1982
Supply
The formulation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) is clear and simple. He said that the problem is inflation and that the answer is unemployment. He said that if we use unemployment as the solution to inflation, we will get recovery. That is the position of the government. No matter who is hurt, the government members say that inflation is the problem, unemployment is the solution, and that is how we get recovery.
All government members may not take this position. A number of ministers of the Crown like to ingratiate themselves to any audience. They are willing to say whatever needs to be said in order to gain a friendly crowd. That is particularly the case with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). I should like to read carefully the comments made by the minister in Paris, France, because I do not think the Minister of Finance had an opportunity to review what he said outside the country when he wished to cut a finer figure in a foreign land. On page 2 of his release he said this:
It is often argued by our colleague ministers of finance that restrictive monetary and fiscal policies are necessary to dampen inflation and that reduced inflation will somehow miraculously lead to future growth.
Those comments sound as if they came right out of the mouth of the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Employment and Immigration continued:
But no mechanism by which future growth will be assured is articulated. We are asked to take it on faith that growth will follow. However, we all know, and it is well accepted by all, regardless of political and economic persuasions, that we can have non-inflationary growth only if we augment the capacity of our economies to produce. This means increased investment in plant and equipment-investment which can be encouraged by lower real rates of interest.
This is exactly contrary to the position taken by the Minister of Finance day after day in the House.
The sense of unreality of the Minister of Employment and Immigration is such that he holds a press conference the day before the worst record of unemployment in recent memory, certainly since World War II, is released. He knows, just as night follows day, that those statistics will come out; but every time he holds a press conference the day before, he shoves out some numbers which have no reality on the street and does not show up in the House for questioning the next day.
I should like to talk about the Minister of Employment and Immigration a little longer, because he is the one who has taken on the public relations role for cabinet. The cabinet has nothing to say to ease the economic pain of Canadians, but it embarked upon a fairly energetic public relations program. Of course, the Minister of Employment and Immigration stars in that role. After the minister's meeting yesterday with recipients of the work sharing program, after meeting with his rented audience, as reported in The Globe and Mail, he said that he does not understand why business and labour do not like work-sharing. He said that they were "almost Pavlovian".
I do not know what he meant by that, but he went on to say that it was "a kind of psychosis on the part of Canadians to get down on everything". He said that those who have critical comments about work sharing suffer from this phychosis. He is so enamoured of the program that he wants to make it a
permanent program to deal with unemployment. He has received an enormous amount of publicity on the program.
It is worthwhile mentioning that the total program covers almost 14,000 people, in relation to an unemployment problem which is in the order of 1.3 million. Also it is worth while looking at the people who have opposed the work-sharing program and why they did so. First, traditionally the work sharing program was opposed by the advisory council to the unemployment insurance fund and by officials within the minister's department. Also it was opposed by the Canadian Labour Congress, the president of CLC and Mr. Clifford Pilkey, president of the Ontario Federation of Labour. It has been described as "sharing the misery". It was opposed by Mr. Stan Roberts when he spoke for the business community as president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. It was rejected by most countries in the western world. For example, in Germany, where they have had the program for some time, they are desperate to get out of most of it if they can. There are good reasons for the opposition.
Let me tell the House what the minister has to sell, what he keeps flogging. Everyone would rather have half a job than no job at all; every company would like to stay alive rather than have to go under. The minister is on solid ground when he says that the people who get it like it. That is for sure, because the alternative is nothing for the worker and bankruptcy for the company. This is why they like it, but there are problems with work sharing. This is why even those who have said "go", have said it cautiously.
The program should only be temporary, if we have it at all. It begins to institutionalize work sharing so that it becomes part of the way in which people see the economy. People become accustomed to the idea that having half a job is about what they can expect. It creates a distortion for the unemployment insurance fund, the purpose of which is to provide a financial bridge when people go from one job to another. It is a clear misuse of the original intention of the fund.
Also it is unfair to those who cannot collect unemployment insurance. There have been many debates in the House concerning the fact that people have to qualify for unemployment insurance. If one happens to be one of the lucky 14,000 who will obtain the benefits of the program for a short time, it is fine; but if one is a labourer and not one of the 14,000, one will not receive it. You could work three days a week and not get unemployment insurance because you have to abide by the waiting period. It is not fair to all, and being fair is the purpose of the fund. Indeed, the fund is not the government's fund; the money comes from workers and from businesses. The program not only distorts the fund, it not only gets people used to the idea that they are only entitled to half a job, but it distorts the government's real task. It masks and creates an illusion around the real task of producing an environment for investment so that full-time, long-term jobs can be created. That is the final problem.
April 8, 1982

The minister, whenever he makes an announcement, should be reminded, and he should remind himself, that all he is doing is putting up a stop-gap solution for people who cannot help themselves. They get a half a job for three or six months and that is all. Basically the minister is saying that that is the way we are going to deal with unemployment in this country. The minister is making a political career out of the misery of people who are caught in a bind. It is one thing to have to do it, but a little more humility on his part would be more in keeping.
The work-sharing program is an example of what the government is doing. It is an example of the government saying to itself and to the Canadian people: "We have nothing to offer. Basically the problem is inflation. We cannot do much about it. We will have to wait until the Americans do something and maybe we will get involved with the Americans." That has been the program and the policy of this government. The recovery which the minister keeps talking about, whenever we get rid of inflation, is not something that will happen automatically. If we are to have a recovery, we have to be prepared for it. The preparation has to be done now, but the government is not preparing. That is why our motion condemns the government.
First, we condemn this government because it brought in a budget that took the guts out of the investment system in this country, the system which creates jobs. We condemn the government because it continues to refuse either to withdraw the budget or to change it. The government has received representation after representation from ordinary Canadians from one end of the country to another, yet it will not change the budget. The government stands in the face of need on an ideology that is mystifying to anybody who hears it. That is our first reason for condemning this government with respect to lack of jobs and employment opportunities in this country.
The second reason we condemn this government is because if we are ever going to have a recovery and if we are going to prepare for it, some sense of co-operation between labour, management and government has to take place. Rather than pursue that course, a course which Canadian governments of one sort or another have had to pursue for 150 years, this government chooses the reverse. Not only does it choose to try to separate, divide and take advantage of the splits between labour and management, but it even takes advantage of splits in the labour movement to try and split the labour movement itself.
In this connection I have an example to give. Three and a half years ago, the Canadian Labour Congress and the Business Council on National Unity, representing the business community, made a proposal initially, I believe, to the then minister of labour and the then minister of employment and immigration. Things went along fairly well for about a year. In the last two years nothing but stalling has taken place. If hon. members speak to representatives of the Business Council on National Unity and representatives of the Canadian Labour Congress, they will learn that the program is being stalled by
Supply
this government. What is important about that is not specifically the program itself, which would monitor the need for specific kinds of skills to be developed in Canada and so create an environment for the production of programs for the learning of those skills-not an unimportant matter-but the opportunity it provides for business and labour to come together. They do not come together very often or very easily, but they did decide to come together on employment need. This government has been diddling them for two years and has paid no attention to them. The situation will get worse because, in the end, both the Canadian Labour Congress and the Business Council on National Unity have found out what the government is up to. They do not trust the government any more.
Third, we condemn the government for the lack of job opportunities and for high unemployment. While the federal government is trying to split labour, trying to split labour from management and both from government, it has also done this before on issues involving the federal government and the provinces of Canada. The government has tried to pick off the provinces one by one and divide them. That is true with respect to training programs. The Minister of Employment and Immigration brought forward a training program. He announced it first. The day before he announced it he took aim at the provinces. He blamed the provinces for everything. He therefore ensured that the training program which is so badly needed in this country would have to be discussed in an atmosphere of animosity and not in an atmosphere of cooperation. If there is ever going to be any kind of a training program or an industrial economic strategy in this country, it must be brought about in an atmosphere of co-operation. This government finds that the only politics it knows is to divide. This government is bereft of solutions. The only thing it knows how to do is to make sure there is division, which enables it to pick off the parts one by one.
Finally, we condemn this government because it has had absolutely no sense of urgency nor has it given any sense of purpose to Canadians during the time it has been in office. This morning I thought about a book written by Jean Vanier, the son of the late Governor General of Canada. The book is entitled "Community and Growth". It is a book that I would recommend to hon. members on the other side. In his book, Mr. Vanier made the point that to become a community there must be concern for everyone in it and Canada would only become a community when there is concern for all of the people in it. Mr. Vanier writes that a community becomes one when all the members of that community and the government have a sense of urgency. He goes on:
There are too many people in the world who have no hope. There are too many cries which go unheard. There are too many people dying in loneliness.
What grates most people is the lost sense of purpose and the lost sense of urgency, as though there were nothing else left to do in this country except wait around for the Americans to deliver what the Liberals cannot. Maybe the Liberals should be reminded that there are forests and lakes to rejuvenate; there are houses to construct; there is land to cultivate; there are roads to pave; there are railroads to build; there are

April 8, 1982

resources to explore; there is steel to forge; there are pipelines to build; there is land to develop; there are towns to expand; there is technology to discover; there are ships to construct; there are factories to remodel; there are bridges to erect; and our vast northern wilderness is yet to be tapped. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to join with the Conservative Party in condemning the government for the foolishness we have been witnessing in this country for the better part of the last two years.
I have wondered a lot about unemployment for at least the last half dozen years, watching as industries close in various parts of the province of Ontario initially, and then when I came here to Ottawa watching as those closings spread from Ontario right across the country. There can be no more difficult time in people's lives than when they lose their job. I do not mean simply being laid off. Many of us have been laid off for short periods of time because of a downturn in the industry we work in. I am talking about the hardship and heartache which is experienced and felt by individuals and their families when a plant closes its doors for the last time.
As I look at many of the people who come into my constituency office to speak with me, I can imagine the upset they feel when, having spent five, ten, in some cases 15 or 20 years working for a particular industry, they find that all of that effort and involvement is for naught. Their industry is no longer required in this grand scheme of things designed by that government in concert with many other governments around the world. Individuals give of their very best, work diligently and make every conceivable effort to produce the things they were asked to produce to the very best of their ability, only to be faced through no fault of their own with the prospect that not only can they no longer return to work in that plant, but as they go to Manpower offices and visit other plants they discover they are not an isolated case. They discover they are but one of tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of people in the same situation.
Then, Mr. Speaker, they find that if they are to survive they must consider moving, to another community nearby if they are lucky, or somewhere else in their province if they are less fortunate, or perhaps to some other part of the country if they have a marketable skill. Some even have to consider uprooting their families and moving away from Canada altogether in order to earn a living and provide for their families. To do that willingly is one thing, although it is a difficult decision at any time; but to have to do it at a time when you have been rendered literally destitute and you had no plans to do so is mind destroying, to say the least.
I put to the government and the minister-one of only two government members here at the moment-that the government has a responsibility for what has happened in this country. The government cannot simply say, as it tends to want to say, that what has happened in Canada has happened all over the world and there is nothing it can do about it; that it is really the fault of the United States because most of our markets are there; or we are in the midst of a worldwide recession and therefore all Canadians must be willing to accept that the recession will out of necessity deprive Canadian workers and their families of a fair opportunity to earn a living.
I reject that because I happen to believe today, as I have believed for years, that it is possible to create in Canada job opportunities by building those things Canadians need. I believe it is possible to use the resources we have in such abundance not only to build the things that Canadians need, but to provide at reasonable cost those same products to people in other parts of the world. I think the reason we are faced with these problems is not because of an inability of Canadians to do the job or generate the need; it has to do with the inability of the government to separate out those things required for domestic consumption from those things influenced directly by international affairs.
I went back, Mr. Speaker, and thought of the hope we had of only two years ago. I looked at the Speech from the Throne and read some of the suggestions the government was making through the Governor General at the time regarding what Canadians had the right to expect from their government. The speech said:
Canadians expect much of this Parliament.
They can expect much. It continued:
-to promote a national development policy that will provide jobs, stimulate growth, build upon regional strengths, and increase Canadian ownership and control of our economy;
I ask you, where are those initiatives today when they are most needed? Where are those initiatives Canadians were led to believe they could expect when we find close to two million people looking for work? Where are these initiatives to promote and develop a national policy to provide jobs, stimulate growth, and help build regional strengths?
The throne speech went on to say in its nice little way "my government", that being the government of the Governor General because it is certainly not my government, I will have you know, Mr. Speaker.
Not the government of the people.

Is it not an injustice that people who have worked all their life should find that, because of this government's policies, they are unable to continue to work in order to earn a living and provide for their families?
Is it not an injustice when a select group within society comprising those two million unemployed is to be asked to shoulder the burden while so many others at the upper end of the scale, such as the banks and the financial institutions, are able to reap such monumental rewards as the result of this government's economic policies?
The government went on to state that Canadians recognize the need to live within their national means, and that they understand the state cannot meet every demand in so doing. I want to say to Your Honour, who knows this fact as well as anyone, that there is no Canadian who expects the state to meet every demand. All that Canadians are asking for is a fair chance to put their labour on the line, a fair chance to go to work, to earn a living and to produce the kinds of products that their friends and neighbours need. There are few, if any, Canadians who are asking that the state look after them daily. There are few Canadians who are suggesting for one moment that they would rather sit at home and do nothing than to go work. Even to suggest that that might be in the minds of a significant number of Canadians is to do the people of Canada an injustice.
Then, of course, the throne speech went on to state that one of the essential objectives of this government is to put more people to work. I say to Your Honour, to hon. members of the House of Commons who are listening here and to anyone else who happens to turn on the television and see this debate by accident, that if that were one of the objectives of the government in April of 1980, then it has failed. It has failed, not because of the actions of others, but because of the pursuit of its own economic policy of high interest rates which has greatly destroyed the manufacturing sector in this country.
There is a hardly a community in any part of the country, no matter where one goes in any province from coast to coast, from north to south, in which one will not find people who are unemployed as a result of the high interest rate policy being pursued by this government, and by the governor of the Bank of Canada on behalf of this government. The government had the effrontery to suggest on April 14, 1980, that one of the essential objectives of the government was to put more people to work. However, it then systematically set about to make it impossible for those self-same people to find employment, to make it virtually impossible for those self-same people not only to find employment, but keep the employment they already had. For the government to do this was to make a mockery of

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
There can surely be no doubt left in the mind of the Minister of Finance that to continue to escalate interest rates can only have a detrimental effect in the battle against inflation. speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been listening very attentively to the comments made by the member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) and the member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans).
After listening to these two speeches, I must admit I am somewhat perplexed, especially since we are extremely lucky in our parliamentary system to have what are known as opposition days. We on the government side of the House are still hoping against hope that some day, the members opposite will have the courage of their convictions as well as the intelligence to produce solutions to the questions they are raising. I hoped this would happen this morning, especially considering the personalities of the two members who spoke earlier.
As I said before, I listened attentively to the member for Rosedale who deployed a vast amount of rhetoric in an attempt to prove that the government was doing nothing about the unemployment problem in Canada, that we were obsessed with inflation and that our only solution was unemployment. Mr. Speaker, I feel that it is unworthy of any member who has given the slightest thought to the economic situation to profer such falsehoods. In trying to recall what the member for Rosedale said, all I can remember is an enormous void and comments that were partisan and lacked any consideration for the real problems confronting Canadians in these difficult times.
As for the member for Hamilton Mountain, he made an excellent speech which reflected a real interest in, and awareness of, the personal problems caused by the economic situation. I agree when he says we want all Canadians to be able to have access to employment and we do not want Canadians to worry each month about meeting their payments, and we would like to see all industrial sectors operating at full capacity, so as to provide more and more jobs in the Canadian economy.
However, the member for Hamilton Mountain needed a scapegoat, and so he said that interest rates were at the bottom of all our ills.
Mr. Speaker, it is sad that once again, despite this very important mechanism in Parliament, namely, opposition days, there is a void, because our colleagues opposite have either forgotten or lacked the necessary courage to say what they would do and what they would like the government to do.
Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, we were not waiting for this to happen, and we have been trying to find ways of solving these very complex economic problems. On this side of the House, we are aware that our economy is not entirely isolated from
April 8, 1982

the effects of the world economic situation, that we have trading partners with whom we must do business, and we are also aware of a very simple principle of economics, namely that as soon as demand for our products drops, there will be a direct impact on industrial activity in a number of regions in Canada. Unfortunately, the impact is often quite sudden.
Mr. Speaker, what we are trying to do is to create conditions that will make it possible to turn around the Canadian economy, and we are doing so in close collaboration with our major foreign trading partners.
What programs have we developed to promote such conditions? First of all, I would like to remind the House that the government has set aside $365 million for the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program or ILAP. As everyone knows, this amount will be used to promote industrial reorganization, manpower training and labour mobility. It is specifically designed for those industrial sectors most affected by technological change or international competition. We have already designated 10 Canadian communities and identified two industries under this program. For the information of the House, these 10 communities are Tracy-Sorel, Port Cartier, Sept-!les, Schefferville, Asbestos in the Eastern Townships, all in Quebec, Sydney in Nova Scotia, Windsor, Brantford, Chatham and Kitchener in Ontario, and McAdam in New Brunswick. The two industries specifically identified under the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program are the automotive parts and home appliance industries. As concerns home appliances, hon. members will be aware that, in the last three weeks, the designation of this industrial sector under the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program has enabled Inglis to take over Admiral, thus consolidating and creating 960 jobs in communities which greatly needed them, including one with which we are very familiar in Quebec, the community of Montmagny.
In addition to this $65 million program now under way, the government has announced the creation of a new adjustment program to ensure the viability and competitivity of the Canadian textile and clothing industries. When we announced this policy and the creation of the CIRB, or Canadian Industrial Renewal Board, we allocated an operating budget of $250 million to the CIRB to provide assistance to the textile and clothing industries and to the communities where they are most concentrated and which now have a high rate of unemployment because of industrial reorganization. We later announced that $17 million would be added to this $250 million envelope for plant modernization, training and manpower mobility in the footwear and tanning industry. Mr. Speaker, we are trying to gear our capacity for action to those sectors and communities which are most affected, in order to solve the specific problems mentioned by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). As this period of economic difficulty affects some sectors more directly than others, we want to direct our action towards those sectors.
Supply

In respect of automotive products, the government has designated so far Windsor, Chatham and Brantford under the ILAC program, the one I explained earlier. Furthermore, the government has announced a special $25 million fund for independent auto parts producers. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, we have negotiated agreements with Chrysler, Ford, Kaydee, Volkswagen, leading to expected new direct investments of over $1 billion and creating over 15,000 direct jobs in these companies.
We also sponsor all through the year 25 to 30 major trade fairs and missions and provide export opportunities to individual Canadian firms. In addition to that, some $50 million in loan guarantees and recoverage contributions have been made available to auto parts companies over the past two years through the enterprise development program and the defence industry productivity program. Finally, purchases under the automotive components remission orders now run at about $115 million a year.
The extent of federal activity is unprecedented. It represents a very substantial effort by the federal government to ensure that the environment within which the industry operates is conducive to sound business decisions which will result in increased investment, production and exports and lead to increased employment opportunities for Canadians.

In addition to the special programs I have announced, and our particular commitments to the automotive industry and export promotion-I mentioned the PEMD program which aims at helping Canadian businesses find new markets,-we established the special mixed funding program last year with an allocation of more than $900 million to help Canadian businesses compete on foreign markets. That program has enabled us to win contracts which are of prime importance to this country's industrial development. I am referring in particular to the Mexico subway contract, that will allow public transit equipment companies to develop new technologies, penetrate new markets and create jobs at home. In addition, we are committed to the development of every region. For the current fiscal year 1982-83, the main estimates of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will be $772 million to promote regional economic growth during this year. This includes over $167 million for grants and $116 million for programs such as the comprehensive plan for Prince Edward Island or the special plan for the development of Magdalen Islands and special ARDA agreements.
Our concern for business throughout Canada will become apparent in the new aspect the programs will take on, once the integration of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Regional Economic Expansion is completed. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced earlier this year, when referring to

April 8, 1982
Supply
government re-organization, the emphasis will be hard on industrial regional development. The merging of the regional offices and programs of DREE and Industry, Trade and Commerce will give Canadian businessmen and women over the coming months better access to the economic programs of the Canadian government and also the opportunity to avail themselves more fully of the business expansion programs, which are centered on innovation.
Mr. Speaker, while recognizing the problems now facing the Canadian economy, the government is quite confident about the potential for economic development of this country. Thus, the Defence Industry Productivity Program, the DIPP, as is commonly called, promotes the economic growth and technological capacity of Canada through the development and production of defence equipment and related products in Canada. In practical terms, what does DIPP mean in the every day life of the workers? It means research grants such as those given for example to the Pratt & Whitney Aircraft of Canada Ltd., in the Montreal area, to Canadair Co., to the de Havil-land Aircraft of Canada Ltd. in Toronto or to Rolls Royce in the Montreal for the area purpose not only of developing advance technologies, but also of making sure that our large manufacturing companies are in a position to maintain their present employment level, to meet international competititon and to find new markets, because we want our country to be a leader in advance technologies and skilled jobs.
Hon. members might remember that during the last fiscal year, we managed twice to increase the DIPP budget, the first time by $20 million and the second time by $27 million, so that the estimates for 1982-83 will be $129 million strictly earmarked to assist companies in developing new technologies or new products and in seeing that highly skilled jobs are made available to Canadians.
Hon. members will also recall that earlier this year, sometime during the third or fourth week in January, the government announced a program to assist greater productivity by technical means. That program is known as STEP. It will help the Canadian industry to take advantage of the outstanding possibilities offered by the electronic revolution. The new program will provide $87.5 million from the former special electronic fund plus an additional amount of $52 million over a three-year period, to help promote the manufacturing and use of electronic and high-technology equipment in the Canadian industry, with the view to improving its productivity and competitiveness in world markets. In other words, additional funds have been provided for the establishment of four new microelectronic centres in Canada, so that each and every Canadian province will now have at one of its universities a high-technology research centre, in the field of microelectronics. In addition, the program also provides for the setting up of an investment fund specifically for major projects in the electronic and equipment industry. Moreover, this program includes a special research and development fund for the manufacture of advance technology production equipment, such as robots and computerized manufacturing equipment.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, the Support for Technology Enhanced Productivity program, or STEP, provides new assistance to businesses in every industry using such products and technologies so that they can get the information they need on electronics and put these technologies and products to good use. Time does not allow me to dwell on the subject but other speakers on this side of the House will have the opportunity to add to my comments later today. However, hon. members do know the significance we attach to the industrial fallback of the megaprojects in every region of Canada, and these fallbacks and their geographic distribution throughout the regions is a priority objective of this government. It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that Canada's vast natural resources and the related secondary manufacturing sectors, as well as manufacturing activities in the areas of engineering, aerospace science, communications, computer science and urban transport equipment will remain the main moving forces of industrial growth in Canada. Innovation in the development of new products and processes will provide new trading opportunities to the Canadian industry on the domestic and foreign markets. However, perhaps for the first time in the history of Canada's economic development, every region will have an opportunity to play an equal role in these developments.

We recognize, of course, that the resource sector and other sectors in the economy, such as some industrial sectors, are experiencing lay-offs and we do not deny that this distressing situation has fallen particularly hard upon some regions in Canada like the forest industry sector in British Columbia and Quebec. Most of these downturns arise from economic conditions prevailing in the foreign markets of the Canadian forest industry, and the situation will not be alleviated until these markets recover. I point out that as a trading nation this is Canada's lot, because without the potential of foreign markets, and if those foreign markets are not open to our products, we cannot expect to be able to weather the storm completely during this difficult period.
The fact is that positive government action has restructured the important forest industry into a position of fundamental strength, whatever its short-term situation. The amount expended under the pulp and paper modernization program has been $276 million, and this has led to further provincial assistance totalling $241 million and private sector investments estimated at between $3 billion and $4 billion, raising industry productivity by 18 per cent. Efforts through DREE to strengthen and expand the resource base through forest management totalled about $91 million last fiscal year. Energy programs developed and implemented by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and DREE have helped forestry to reduce its energy consumption by the impressive total of 20 per cent. New overseas markets for Canadian products are
April 8, 1982

being obtained through a variety of effective trade initiatives. In this sector I think the story is a strong one.
Positive steps have also been taken to create and sustain jobs directly.

The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) recently announced the allocation of $140 million to a job creation program aimed at hiring people now receiving unemployment insurance benefits, to work in reforestation and fishery projects. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crom-bie) referred to the work-sharing program with an irony which is incongruous in view of the situation, but considering that the government has announced nearly $350 million of new programs aimed solely at job creation in the last six weeks, to say that these are just bandaid measures, as the hon. member for Joliette told me behind the curtains, is somewhat of an exaggeration.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with the charges of chronic failure made by the hon. member for Rosedale. The programs which I have just listed and the great economic potential of our country encourage us, on this side of the House, to meet today's economic challenge optimistically. Mr. Speaker, I wanted to give a brief summary of the policies developed by the government of Canada to meet that challenge. I could also have described in fuller detail all the job creation programs we have implemented, but others will have the opportunity to do so this afternoon. However, as the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) pointed out at the end of his speech, we on this side of the House also believe that people must be our first concern and that our policies must be aimed at promoting the welfare of Canadians.
[English)

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to dwell today on the abysmal failure of this government nor the frightening statistics with which we are continually bombarded. It is my intention to attempt to bring a positive note to this debate.
In my own life I have always found that one of the major keys to success in business is to learn by example. You seek information and use ideas from those who are successful and incorporate them in your own venture. The government of this country does not seem to appreciate this simple principle. It does not even seem to be able to learn from the example of failure. In this respect I am thinking in particular of Great Britain, the economy of which has been sliding downhill for a number of years. We seem to be only a few short steps behind that once proud and industrious nation in its headlong plunge to economic ruin.
Why cannot we-as a country or, more specifically, as a government-take a look at countries which are successful in today's world? Let us look at Japan, for instance. Every Canadian knows that Japan is presently in much better economic state than we are. Can we not learn why and make use of this information? What allows Japan, a resource-poor
Supply
collection of islands, to outstrip Canada, a country virtually floating in a sea of valuable resources?
Japan has the most formidable economy in the world today, second in size only to that of the U.S.A. While our economy sluggishly plods along under the burden of declining productivity, a huge national debt, high interest rates and doubledigit inflation, the Japanese economy defies world trends and continues to move ahead by leaps and bounds. We live right next door to our major market; the Japanese have to ship across the Pacific Ocean. Our economy was left intact after the Second World War; that of Japan was devastated as a result of its war effort.
What does account for the difference between our two countries? When viewing statistics it soon becomes clear that Japanese productivity outstrips that of any other western economy. In 1979, Japanese productivity rose by 13 per cent and in 1980 by another 9 per cent. At the same time this was happening, the west saw unit labour costs increasing, in the U.S. by 11 per cent, in West Germany by 5 per cent and in Great Britain by 20 per cent. This past year Canada was racked by labour unrest, which will undoubtedly show up as a further decline in our productivity.
It was long assumed that Japanese workers were paid comparatively low wages. This may have been true in the 1950s and 1960s, but it is now estimated that by the 1990s Japanese per capita income will be almost twice that of its American counterpart. It is evident that labour cannot shoulder the full responsibility for declining productivity in Canada. No, the source of the Japanese phenomenon goes deeper than that. It is profoundly concerned with the basic attitudes of government, management and labour.
To deal with government first, the Japanese government operates quite differently from what Canadians experience. Although the political structures are similar-both are parliamentary democracies-the role of government is an interesting study in contrasts. Japanese government bureaucracy is small in relation to the population and the size of the Japanese economy. The reason for this is that government, like all sectors of the Japanese economy, is output oriented. In Canada it seems that government is growth oriented.
In addition, we are currently going through a phase in which the government is intervening to an ever greater degree in the private sector. Proof of this is evident in policies such as the National Energy Program. It is likely that in the 1980s we will see a continued and unprecedented assault on other sectors of the economy by the federal Liberal government.
As an example of differing attitudes in government, it is worthwhile to examine how government involves itself in the private sector in Japan and here in Canada. In Japan the ministry of international trade and industry only supports industries with long-term growth potential. The Japanese see the death of an industrial sector or a company as part of the natural life cycle of the economy. But what do we do here? We bail out companies like Chrysler, Massey-Ferguson and Cape Breton Steel. Once we start to prop up an ailing industry, we

are stuck with it forever. It becomes parasitic, sucking the vitality out of our economy.
In this respect we need only look as far as England to see the devastating effect this has on western economies. British Steel, for example, drained $1.5 billion out of the British economy last year. That was $1.5 billion for one industry. The Japanese would have spent that money on growth industries, which would have created long-term, productive jobs. Basically the Japanese government looks ahead; ours looks behind. Japan spends 25 per cent of its gross national product on government; Canada and Britain spend 40 per cent plus of their gross national product on government. That comparison alone speaks volumes about the state of our economy. We are an expensively overgoverned society. We look at multi-levels of government for support at any excuse, and seem to feel more secure with bureaucrats dogging our every move. Government has invaded every facet of our life. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, Parliament is even now in the last throes of a complete loss of control over the bureaucracy. Once it becomes uncontrollable, it will be the end of private enterprise in this country.
In Japan, government seems to work side by side with business and not as its antagonist. When people talk about the Japanese economic miracle, the ministry of international trade and industry is always mentioned. There is no question that this ministry has continually been behind the thrust pushing Japanese industry to the forefront. In Canada, the government seems to see industry as profiteers and exploiters of the Canadian worker rather than a source of employment and income. Business is constantly under attack. I need not mention more than the November MacEachen budget.
A recent example of government attitudes occurred in Ontario. The Volkswagen company wanted to set up a plant in Barrie, Ontario, partially as a result of government incentives. Barrie was the ideal location for Volkswagen because it could purchase an already developed site and it would be close to major markets. The federal government, however, decided that it wanted the plant in either Montreal or Windsor. Coincidentally, all Montreal seats are held by Liberals and three Liberal cabinet ministers come from Windsor. The government declared that if Volkswagen did not build in one of these two cites, then funding would be withdrawn. So Volkswagen said: "Okay, we will set up a plant in the U.S.". Finally the government relented and allowed Volkswagen to build in Barrie. So you can see that even before the plant was set up, the government was taking a confrontationist stance with the company. You can be assured that other companies will consider the Volkswagen experience when thinking about operating in Canada.
This is only part of the problem with our style of government involvement with industry. In Japan, research and development lies at the heart of productivity increases and ultimately is the foundation of the economic miracle. In general, Canadians seem to fear change. They look at advances like robotization of assembly lines and think of job
losses. What they do not realize is that whether they lose their jobs to robots or whether they lose them because they are no longer competitive, they are still unemployed. The difference is that if they lose their jobs to technological advance, there will likely be other jobs available. As hundreds of thousands of Canadians can attest today, being uncompetitive simply leaves them collecting a UIC cheque or welfare.
Retraining would allow workers to escape the drudgery of boring and repetitive jobs and allow them to move on to higher levels of skill that have the potential of being much more rewarding. The point to remember is that in Japan, the level of unemployment is significantly lower than in Canada. No one should fear change when obsolescence is the enemy.
In Canada, we spend about 0.9 per cent of our GNP on research and development, while Japan has already exceeded 3 per cent. Japan has 36 research and development workers per
10,000	population, a figure 50 per cent higher than the United States. More than any other single factor, this accounts for Japanese productivity and the strength of her economy.
In Canada, we have yet to recognize and act upon this fact. We rank only above Iceland and Ireland in research and development spending. The government offers little incentive to private industry to expand research and development facilities. The Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) recently set 1.5 per cent of GNP by 1985 as a goal for research spending, but this assumed massive private sector input which is unlikely to appear, especially in light of recent budgetary measures. That would leave us just slightly above our peak of ten years ago. Proposed cutbacks in funding for post-secondary educational institutions will further worsen the situation.
What is required is a co-ordination of research and development efforts by the universities, government centres and the private sector. Combined with this co-ordination of effort must be at least a doubling of current funding from all sources. This would still leave us about 1.2 per cent below Japan, but at least we would be approaching the levels of other industrialized nations. To skimp on research funding is false economy.
Also, if Canadians hope to succeed they must co-operate with each other. In this country labour is set against management, the public sector is fighting the private sector, and the federal government wars with the provinces. Government should work with business to develop opportunities which will in turn create jobs and strengthen the economy. Japan has thrived on this sort of co-operation.
I would like to outline briefly the sort of progress Japan has made as a result of this approach to economic development. Right now in Japan some 50,000 university students are studying various aspects of micro-electronic technology. In the United States there are perhaps 2,500 students in this field many of whom, I would bet, are students from Japan. I hesitate to think about how many we have in Canada- perhaps 50 or 100?
Let us examine the result of this emphasis on micro-electronic technology. Japan has 80,000 robots, nearly three

quarters of the world's total. While we scramble to introduce robots to our auto assembly lines-probably the most basic level at which they would be used-the Japanese are using robots to produce more robots. As a matter of fact, the Japanese view the auto industry as a dying sector to be passed on to less developed nations-such as Canada, no doubt. Ten per cent of Japanese robots are rated as intelligent because they can sense an object, grasp it and place it where it belongs with a precision requiring more than simply mechanical movement.
The Japanese are presently working on a factory run by computers and laser beams. Depending on how the computer is programmed, the material that goes into the processor will come out as anything from a home appliance to a child's toy or a car muffler. Who is developing this process? It is the Japanese ministry of international trade and industry. It suggests that this process, known as flexible manufacturing, will soon allow small factories to turn out a large variety of products without requiring humans to leave their control rooms. The ministry will pass this technology on to the private sector. This is how to create jobs, not through a system of grants that create positions simply as a political response to unemployment statistics.
In the field of computers, five Japanese manufacturers now have 40 per cent of the world market in random access memory chips. Two Japanese companies are now laying claim to having the fastest computer in the world, thanks to new semiconductor technology. Soon they expect to have computers that respond to voice commands and are able to read charts and graphs.
Not only do the Japanese want to transmit information quickly, they also want to move people and material quickly. The famed "bullet train" is definitely old hat in Japan; it only travels at 200 kilometres per hour. The Japanese have already had a test train at Kyushu travel 10 centemetres above the ground at up to 514 kilometres per hour, or about 320 miles per hour. By the late 1990s, these trains-riding silently on a super-conducting magnetic levitation railway system-will be in regular operation. What is more, the Japanese borrowed this technology from the Germans who are well aware of the value of research and development.
So why does the government have this negative attitude, this approach that obviously destroys economic growth? The first reason is the one I have already mentioned-it fears new technologies. The second has to do with its socialist tendencies. The government is more concerned with distributing wealth we do not have, then in creating wealth that is our life's blood. We allow government programs to take priority over growth initiatives. Programs that would create wealth are downgraded. Social programs are important; we have a real and growing responsibility to help the elderly, the disabled and the handicapped. No one will argue with that. Encouraging business to expand would reduce unemployment while at the same time increasing the tax base, so that we could afford needed social services.

Finally, I should like to discuss Japanese management techniques. Canadian labour and management could take a few pointers from their counterparts across the Pacific. In Japan salary is closely connected with productivity, while Canadian labour tries to tie wage increases to the rate of inflation. The former technique would actually dampen inflation while helping workers to identify more closely with the success of the company. This raises company morale, which in itself is a productivity booster. Connecting wage increases to the CPI is ludicrous because it fuels further inflation, and a measure derived from price increases of a general basket of goods has little application to a specific industry.
In Japan bonuses make up 30 per cent or more of a worker's wages. Wages increase as years of service to the company accumulate. These measures provide a real incentive to workers to stay with their job, thus reducing employee turnover in the company. With wages getting largely determined by productivity, workers become eager for technological changes which will improve their per capita output without requiring an increase in worker input. Absenteeism declines significantly under this system.
Japan is not a perfect state but there is much we could learn from the Japanese. Instead of setting up trade barriers which encourage the continuation of obsolete industry, we should work with the Japanese, learn from them, and compete with them at their own game. This is precisely what the Japanese did to the West. Instead of complaining about unfair competition, we should realize the incredible potential of Canada. Others are following in Japan's footsteps; Korea, Singapore, Taiwan and Hong Kong are all stars on the rise. We will have to compete with them or be left behind in a self-imposed morass of economic and social problems.
