Under the circumstances, I must nevertheless remind the House that, as an elected representative of the province with the worst unemployment record and as the member for Joliette, I am not the only one to condemn the government. During a FPU meeting held last week, farmers by the thousands severely condemned the government for leaving them at the mercy of interest rates. As I said earlier this week to the Prime Minister, I hope they will not blame high interest rates on the Quebec government. I think this is clearly a federal responsibility and is due to the government's high interest rates policy which is affecting adversely farmers, small and medium-sized businesses and contractors.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that if the government had shown a little sensitivity to the needs of these major industries, it could have easily favoured these key industries, thereby averting the current problems and distress. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) was right when he compared the programs announced by the government to misery-sharing. The government is trying to maintain and stabilize poverty through programs. Canadians will be offered a 4-day week, with paid leave on the fifth day, as well as early retirement at age 50. Mr. Speaker, you doubtless know just as well as I do that this is not the way to build a country, to make it strong and able to withstand any attack against its security. This is unthinkable. Because of its bad administration, the government is clearly stuck and it keeps on announcing investments by hundred million dollars in an attempt to correct a situation in which it placed Canadians and alleviate a bankruptcy which is surely unacceptable to the Canadian people.
So, when Quebec farmers complain, other industries are involved. The government is being condemned for its lack of policy planning in the automobile industry, the tremendous problems facing small and medium-sized businesses as well as the construction industry, and the measures introduced are not likely to help the economy recover. If it had provided home owners with the assistance we suggested, thousands of those who are experiencing mortgage renewal problems would be in a much better position, and thousands of other Canadians would have become home owners, thereby saving a great many jobs, something members opposite are perfectly aware of. As far as the soft industries in my province are concerned, Mr. Speaker, we know the difficulties they encounter on a daily

April 8, 1982
Supply
basis, but the government allowed these industries also to deteriorate. If the minister responsible were honest, he would confess that in spite of the steps the government has taken for the footwear industry, for instance, through retraining or early retirement programs, he has completely given up on its future survival. It has been clear for the past three or four weeks that this industry will disappear unless steps are taken to include leather shoes within the total quota system.
The minister's answer is overdue. In fact, 6,000 jobs have been lost, 15,000 workers are still worried today. I do not know how many questions I have put-often with the tacit support of some Liberal members who did not dare rise in this House- politely to a parliamentary secretary about what was going to happen. I think they have a responsibility to demand that the minister take action and ensure the survival of that industry. The same could happen in the textile industry, and a number of others. That is the kind of situation we are now facing, and we know thousands of young people are discouraged and worried because they have not yet found a place in the labour market. How can we ensure this country's future with such gigantic failure?
Mr. Speaker, I know other members want to speak on the issue. But I think the time has come to ask members opposite, be they from Quebec or elsewhere, to stop that hypocrisy. Let us demand, as those members have a responsibility to do, that ministers and especially the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) change course. As I said, Mr. Speaker, the damage is done. No political group in 24 hours could correct the damage done by this government over the last 15 years. It would have been possible as late as two years ago to avoid the worst. This government failed to respond to the direction and proposals we set and which would have proved very valuable to save this country from catastrophy. This government is the main culprit, because of its lack of management and vision, its stubborn determination to take the place of private industry and deceive Canadians into believing that fighting inflation will reduce unemployment. I have been hearing that same old cliche for 15 years but we now have both unemployment and inflation. This is utter failure. I will never insist enough on this point.
Today the Minister of Finance gave us another proof he has no compunction about his gigantic failure. He did not even give a hint he will change course or philosophy. And those hon. members opposite keep absolving and supporting him. In my view those people have responsibilities and should in the circumstances, prevail upon the government to change its attitude. We, the official opposition, are convinced, as thousands other Canadians are that this government erred, this government led the country into the doldrums, because thousands of people now suffer and beg this government to show leadership and alter its policies.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, the present government will rely on the same philosophy to lead the country out of the doldrums. It will fail. My submission may be pessimistic, my colleagues opposite may say I am being too gloomy. This may not be too encouraging to the thousands of Canadians who are listening, but unless the Minister of Finance completely changes his
philosophy, the unemployment rate will increase further. And it is my belief that my warning will prove true in the short term. This government led us and keeps leading us astray but apparently does not give a hoot about the thousands of Canadians facing problems because of the current economic situation. Relations between provinces should resume, and at once. Enough stubbornness. Certainly, they will say this comes under provincial, not Canadian or federal jurisdiction. But in my view, men and women should rise to the challenge and reopen negotiations. That at any rate could prove beneficial for the Canadian people as a whole. Despite suggestions of politicking from all parties, I feel we have a responsibility to brace up and together with our provincial partners try to find a way out. But as long as the Minister of Finance-although he indicated this morning, that if he thought this could help the country, he would be prepared to resign. One of the services he could render this country, if he does not want to change his philosophy is to resign, and the sooner the better. He has proved his incompetence and mismanagement. We have here, before us, and especially from my province, 74 out of 75 hon. members who are in cahoots with so inefficient an administration, and are lacking courage under the circumstances.
I dare hope, once again, that the few remarks we are making today on our side of the House will bring this government to reflect seriously upon the hardships and the wrongs it is now inflicting upon the Canadian people, and upon the discouragement that will ensue every day with regard to the future of Canada. The fact remains that the present government is responsible, not so much to exercise power, but to ensure greater wellbeing for Canadians; but it has proved that it is incapable of doing so, for a long time now, and of achieving what this illustrious Prime Minister had promised: a just society. He is now left with two choices: either to change his economic philosophy that does not fit the situation, or simply, honestly, recognize his incompetence, his inability and resign, giving others a chance to do better.

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of the Environment and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
We have been treated this afternoon, Mr. Speaker-and particularly by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken-to a great deal of indignation and emotion. I suppose indignation is the professional responsibility of the opposition-a great deal of heat with very little light. When I listened to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), I thought for a moment that he had joined the New Democratic Party. He was showing such a selfrighteous concern that only he had compassion for those who are unemployed and those who are suffering from our economy. I thought he has verily established his qualifications for joining those who are self-righteous in the ranks of the New Democratic Party.
The question is not self-righteousness, Mr. Speaker. I can assure you and I can assure all members of the House that the
April 8, 1982

members on this side of the House show as much care, as much concern, as much compassion as ever has been indicated by the members sitting opposite. The question is not who cares most, Mr. Speaker; the question is what are the problems that face us, what are the solutions for dealing with them, what are the alternatives presented to us in responding to those challenges?
The motion of the official opposition alleges a chronic failure. A failure can take place only in the context of the opportunities, the challenges and the problems that confront us.
There is no doubt, there is no denying-and there is no lack of concern in care for them, on this side of the House of Commons-that Canada faces difficult economic problems and challenges. But it is fruitless, it is pointless, to contend that those problems stem simply from policies of this government without a recognition of the international context within which Canada's economic policy must be rooted. As long as we are a major trading nation, as we are, and as long as we have capital needs, as we do, we will not be able to escape the impact within our economy of the general world economic situation. We can do better or we can do worse, confronted with any specific situation, but inevitably in Canada we will have to live with the consequences of the economic health of our major trading partners.
The question is, what kind of economic policies should Canada adopt to confront those admittedly difficult and challenging world economic situations? That is exactly where the hon. member for Joliette and the members of the official opposition have fallen down in their responsibility to describe for us some coherent alternative that would make sense to the kinds of policies that this government is pursuing. Quite clearly, this government is pursuing a policy of fiscal and monetary restraint. Is the official opposition suggesting we should abandon that policy? I can say, as a result of a variety of discussions and communications I have had with the private sector, that on the whole the private sector very much wishes the government to maintain fiscal and monetary restraint.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Does he wish lower interest rates? How is he going to have lower interest rates without the imposition of exchange controls or a greatly reduced value of the Canadian dollar? Is that the policy which the official opposition wishes us to pursue? Do they wish us to undertake new programs to combat the social consequences of those economic difficulties that we face? If so, do they intend that we should pay for them through increased taxes or in the expansion of the federal government borrowing requirements?
They are strong in indignation, they are strong in heat, but there is very little in terms of light as to what alternative they would have us choose. Yes, Mr. Speaker, these are difficult times in the Canadian economy and there are hard choices, but they are not hard choices imposed on the people of Canada by the will of the government, they are imposed on us by the international economic situation. Those difficulties will be faced within the Canadian economy as long as we are engaged to the extraordinary degree that we are in world trade, as long
Supply
as we are the advocates, as we are, of freer trade-I say freer, not necessarily freee trade-and as long as we have the kind of capital need that this country requires.
Nevertheless, though I am disappointed in the degree of constructive suggestions flowing from the official opposition, 1 welcome the presentation of this motion. I hope it will lead some further opposition to some precision in what alternative policies he should have us adopt. They are fearlessly opposed to inflation; they are very brave in saying we should not have unemployment; they are courageous in objecting to high interest rates; but they have not put forward any coherent or constructive policy for responding to those problems-different from the basic over-all economic and fiscal strategy the government is following.
I welcome this question put before us, Mr. Speaker, for another reason. It gives me an opportunity to discuss the longterm economic development strategy which was brought forward by the government last November and which, has not in my view been looked at sufficiently by Parliament or by the public. It is perhaps understandable that, in the controversy surrounding the budget, not as much attention has been paid to that document as I think it deserves. I stress the importance of that long-term economic development strategy because the NDP, the Conservatives and we-all of the members in this House, I think-know in our heart of hearts that yes, the Canadian economic situation is largely influenced by the economic health of our trading partners.
I suspect that almost all of us also know that the only way to fight effectively both inflation and unemployment is by enhancing productivity in our economy. If there is any magic wand in economics-and I doubt that there are magic wands-if there is any approach that really makes sense if we are to tackle those twin evils, it is by pursuing policies which enhance productivity within our economy, to make us more competitive, to provide employment, to provide for increased productivity and the ability to counter the effects of inflation.
It is within that context that the economic development strategy was brought forward in November. It is not a blueprint. It does not lay down some sort of nuts and bolts plan that must be followed in every detail. But it does give an indication of the path which the federal government believes should be pursued if we are to maximize the economic potential which the country undoubtedly has, if we are to maximize the growth of our economy.
If I were to single out the aspects of it which 1 think are particularly important and that warrants the attention of the public and the attention of the House, they are three in number. The first that the strategy suggests is that there are key sectors or key areas in which both government and the private sector must focus their efforts if we are to maximize the potential for our economic development. Those key areas are described at the very beginning of the document with emphasis, of course, on resource exploitation because Canada has international competitive advantages in the resource area.

April 8, 1982
Supply
Unfortunately, I think some have interpreted the document as being overly concerned with resources and megaprojects. Undoubtedly, resources are one of the most important base of competitiveness and enhanced productivity within the country. But the strategies do not confine or focus itself simply on the resource base. It goes on to describe other areas of key importance-and these are not in order of importance-such as manufacturing. The high technology industries and the development of technologies themselves.
The importance of the document is, first, that it attempts to describe those areas in which the federal government believes it should concentrate its efforts since they promise the maximization of productivity and growth in the return over the long term. The second aspect of the document which I think is of great importance is the rather new approach it takes to regional development. Regional development policies in the past have been largely, but not exclusively, defined in terms of the need for strengthening slow growth or disadvantaged areas of the country. The conclusion of the government, which is represented in this document, is that within each region of Canada there now are great opportunities and potential for regionalized development. A regional development policy can now effectively combine the need for balanced regional economic development and the support of the key sector strategy for the country. In other words, a regional development policy and economic development policy can go hand in hand. By reinforcing our strengths within the Canadian economy we can maximize growth and at the same time respond to the needs for regional development.
The third aspect of the economic development strategy which I believe deserves attention, because it has not been seen-certainly by members of the opposition-is that it indicates and advocates what the government wants, which is a constructive partnership with the private sector in the development of the Canadian economy. For instance, if one turns to page 11 of the economic development strategy, the section on the government and the private sector, one finds it makes clear the predominant role that the government believes the private sector must play in economic expansion. It emphasizes that it is markets, demand or potential demands which must drive the investments and development of productive capacity within the Canadian economy. It is an emphasis on the fact that it is the private sector which is the engine for economic development with the country.
I have said that what the document expresses clearly is the desire for a constructive partnership between government and private sector. I say "partnership" advisedly. While it is certainly true that the private sector must be the motor force in the exploitation of commercial opportunities which face the country, it is equally true that the government must play a positive and constructive role in that process, particularly in the expenditure of its investments for the strengthening of the infrastructure of the country in manpower training, education, transportation and export development assistance.
There is a variety of areas where the government is necessarily active and where those activities must be designed to focus or create a context of support for the kind of private sector development which will provide the country with the growth that it needs. A desire for a constructive partnership between government and the private sector is the principal motivating force which has led this government to undertake an intensive consultation process with the private sector about the ways in which these development objectives can best be met. Indeed, it is a consultation process for the examination and discussion of those objectives to make them more precise so that the private sector and the government together can make sure that their efforts are in harmony, that they are yoked together rather than playing at cross purposes.
I commend the economic strategy to all members of the House. It is not a blueprint or a nuts and bolts design but it is an indication of the direction the government should follow to maximize our economic potential. Indeed, it charts the way the government has already begun to act.
This can be seen in the redefinition departmental responsibilities for economic expansion and in our external conduct of our economic affairs. For example, it can be seen in the renewed and strengthened emphasis that the federal government is giving to the support of the forestry sector in Canada. It can be seen in the emphasis on high technology development which has been reflected by recent decisions of the federal government to increase funding and support for the space industry by something close to $500 million between now and 1985. It certainly can be seen in the kind of support the federal government is giving to the strengthening and enhancement of science and technology and research and development within our country.
I recommend the economic development strategy to hon. members opposite and to all members of the House. I think hon. members opposite would be surprised to discover how much they agree with that strategy if they would only take the time to read it.
I have mentioned the question of research and development policy and 1 wish to spend a few more moments on that. It was a subject dealt with to some degree by the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) who spoke just a few moments ago. I welcomed very much his intervention and discussion of those issues. I only wish that he could have been a little more carefully informed so that he would have had knowledge of the facts. The undoubted fact of which he does not seem to be particularly aware is that the effort, both in terms of funding by the federal government and the effort which has been made within the private sector since this government took office, has moved us considerably closer to the achievement of major objectives in research and development. I would urge the hon. member before he speaks again in debate to look at the brief description which was sent to him a little over a week ago outlining what has happened over the past two years in the research and development area. It is, as my colleague behind me says, a great story of success and accomplishment, but it is not, however, one about which we
April 8, 1982

should be complacent or smug. There is a great deal to be done yet. We are certainly very much on the path to a greatly improved performance, not only on the part of government but on the part of the private sector as well.
Although it can be somewhat tedious to refer to statistics, I would like to cite three of four paragraphs in this report, given the concern expressed by the hon. member opposite. The report entitled The Government of Canada's Investment in Science which, as I said, appeared just over a week ago indicates how well the country is doing compared with the situation we faced two years ago. Statistics Canada has recently estimated that Canada's gross expenditures on research and development have increased by 34 per cent since 1979. That is from something well over $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion in 1981. That means the percentage of our gross national product devoted to research and development has increased in that period from something over 0.9 per cent to 1.07 per cent. It falls short of the objectives that we hope to achieve by 1985 and which I believe we will achieve. It falls short of what would be an ideal objective for us to achieve downstream from that. The important point is that the downward trend in the proportion of expenditure in research and development as compared to the proportion of the gross national product which was evident throughout the 1970s has been arrested and reversed.
The hon. gentleman questioned the degree to which industry was successfully pursuing increased research and development. The fact is that investment in research and development in that industry during that same period of time has risen by 43 per cent to close to $500 million. That is it has risen $1,034 billion to $1,481 billion between 1979 and 1981. In other words, over a 20 per cent growth rate was achieved in 1981. In real terms, these growth rates are higher than in any period since the early 1960s. That is the performance in the private sector.
Federal government expenditure increases have been significant as well. They have increased by some 34 per cent, close to $500 million, over the same period of time. It has been the objective of our policy, clearly described, that the largest increases should be in the private sector, exactly for the reasons upon which I touched earlier in my discussion of an economic development strategy. We want to see the private sector expand its efforts very considerably because we believe the most effective research and development is that research and development which is guided by the demand opportunities, the market possibilities and the capacity to exploit the market place by those who are commercially sensitive.
In one last comment on this matter, perhaps I should touch upon the fact that the federal government clearly has attached great priority to the research and development side, and that is evident when we compare increases in federal expenditures on research and development with other uses of federal government funds. During the last two years research and development expenditures in the natural sciences increased by almost
Supply
40 per cent. In the same period the government's total operating and capital expenditures for all departments and agencies increased by about 22 per cent. In other words, expenditures directed toward research and the exploitation and enhancement of science and technology are roughly double the general growth level of government expenditures.
Our concern has been clearly demonstrated. Well over a year ago-in January of 1981-when the five-year spending framework of the federal government in relation to science and technology was presented, we established and described the objectives we hoped the university sector and the private sector would achieve. All that was done in January of 1981. Spending targets were established, and spending objectives for the private university sector were, admittedly, ambitious. Some said we would not be able to attain them. The fact is that over the past two years we have generally met the targets and the critical path of expenditure we described at that point.
As I said earlier to my friend, the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), there is no reason for us to remain smug or complacent. I have recently gone to the cabinet with proposals to strengthen our policies which would encourage or entice the expansion of yet further efforts on the part of the private sector. I am happy to be able to say to hon. members that the cabinet has approved the general recommendations we presented and that an action plan for the implementation of those proposals will be worked out over the next few months. Good as the private sector performance has been and good as our support has been, we still believe there is room for improvement in engendering even better private sector performance than there has been to this point.

Mr. Speaker, today is yet another sad day in a series of sad days because of the announcement by Statistics Canada that unemployment has once again reached a record high level. That level is 9 per cent, or 1,228,000 Canadians out of work. Today is doubly sad because we are not at the end of the trend, we are in the middle of the trend. If one were to look at the economic situation in this country, one would realize that there is not even a light at the end of the tunnel. We know that unemployment will increase next month, unfortunately, and it will do so the month after that and so forth, unless some action is taken.
I was somewhat surprised by a statement made by the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Roberts). He mentioned that the government's objective is to enhance productivity. He talked about opportunities and about the private sector. He talked about wanting to expand the efforts of the private sector in order to expand productivity in our economy. It is strange and ironic for a Liberal cabinet minister to utter such high-sounding phrases when it is the present Liberal government which has thrown obstacles in the way of every opportunity to enhance productivity.
The present Liberal government has been in office not just for the last two and a half years but for the last 14 years, and its lack of policies and efforts has strangled opportunities in

April 8, 1982
Supply
the productive industrial sector, the manufacturing sector, the agricultural sector, the small business sector; and the list goes on.
One need not look too far back to see how some of these problems developed. One has merely to go back to the November 12 budget to know that as a result of the policies enunciated in that budget nothing but obstacles have been thrown in the way of progress in a country which has all the opportunities the minister just mentioned. We have better opportunities than most nations in the world. Per capita we are the wealthiest nation in natural resources, in human resources and in technological know-how. We should not be comparing ourselves with other nations which are not blessed with these resources and with the potential productive forces we have in Canada, yet what has happened after years of attempts by this government to get the economy moving? Unemployment has reached a staggering level in this country of opportunity. 1 will cite just a few well-known figures. The current account deficit is $6.6 billion. The deficit in fully manufactured goods-the minister alluded to manufacturing and productivity-is $20.7 billion. Interest and dividends paid to other countries amounted to $7 billion net in 1981 alone. The government spent half a billon dollars in the last month-alone to defend the staggering Canadian dollar. Corporate profits were down 44 per cent in the last quarter of 1981. Manufacturing is operating at its lowest level in 20 years. The list goes on.
Why? It is not because, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said on numerous occasions, the free market or free enterprise system no longer works. It is because the policies, philosophies and programs of this Liberal government do not allow that free enterprise or free market system to operate freely. They strangle it with directives, controls, regulations and a paper-work burden on small business until they strangle and bring the whole economic system and the whole economic base on which this great country of ours was built to their knees.
I repeat that we do not have to go any further for confirmation than that "tremendous" budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) last November 12. Every group of individuals and every organization, be it apolotical, Conservative, New Democratic or Liberal, has condemned the budget. It did not take a step forward to help the employment situation in Canada. Indeed, it took a giant step backward.
Something is wrong when 1.25 million Canadians are unemployed and the government is looking around the world to import labour. Last year 20,000 people were brought in to do special trade jobs, while over a million Canadians were unemployed. There is no program or policy of the Liberal government to deal with the unemployment situation. But worse than that, the programs which exist in specific sectors are not only damaging to the economy of the country but are also fueling unemployment.
If I may, I would like to deal briefly with one very important sector. It is a sector I have been following very closely for the last couple of years. I refer to the automotive industry. In this country the automotive industry is responsible, directly or indirectly, for one out of seven jobs from coast to coast and one
out of six jobs in Ontario. In the last year one third of auto assemblers in this country have either lost their jobs or have been laid off and 40 per cent of auto parts manufacturing workers have lost their jobs in the last year. That is a disgrace, Mr. Speaker and it is a typical example of the inaction of this administration. The same holds true for the appliance manufacturers, the textile industry, the show industry and small business, which is probably potentially the largest employer in any economic sector.
What is the government doing about the auto industry, Mr. Speaker? It claims that it is only the opposition that recommends some sort of action. I am not a protectionist, Mr. Speaker, but when one out of seven jobs in Canada is threatened by the virtual demise of the auto industry, then I think the government must take action.
For two and a half years the government has been negotiating with the Japanese, the Americans and the others who are taking over the industry in this country. Any time my colleagues and I raise this question with the ministers who are responsible, they reply that they are still negotiating. They were negotiating two years ago, and one year ago and last month when the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley) went to Japan, they were negotiating. When he came back he said that he was not concerned that the Japanese did not agree with his proposals because they agreed to negotiate again. In the meantime, tens of thousands of jobs are being lost to that industry in this country. There are ways to get around the problem, Mr. Speaker. There are solutions. Nearly every industrialized nation in the world has found a solution.
We all know that the Japanese have taken over a large part of the North American auto market. In fact, 28 per cent of the Canadian automotive market has been taken over by the Japanese, yet this is virtually the only nation in the industrialized world that does not have some sort of agreement with them. Australia has an 85 per cent local content rule for imported cars; the United Kingdom has a limit of ten per cent on Japanese imports; France has a three per cent limit on Japanese imports; Italy has a limit of only 2,000 units; Spain has a 63 per cent local content rule; Brazil has a 95 per cent local content rule, and the United States has just signed an agreement which will hold Japanese imports to a certain level for a three-year period.
All this government is doing is negotiating, Mr. Speaker, but negotiating what? It is just as if a patient were ill in a hospital and the doctors took time to talk about what they would do with him, but in the meantime the patient died. All the talk in the world will not help him then. What a patient needs is immediate action. The government has not taken immediate action, Mr. Speaker. It has been talking for two and a half years. We saw this coming two and a half years ago, Mr. Speaker. The government saw it coming two and a half years ago and the industry saw it coming two an a half years ago.
April 8, 1982

I am not the only one nor is this party the only party to claim that there are ways the problems can be eliminated or reduced. The Canadian Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association has made very positive recommendations, as has the United Auto Workers Union. I have in my hand a list of resolutions put forward by various town councils, but I shall only put a few on the record. On March 22, 1982, the city of Port Colborne passed a resolution requesting the federal government to limit foreign vehicle imports and to negotiate an agreement to provide for Canadian value-added content of not less than 85 per cent; the city of Oshawa had the same thing as did the town of Lincoln and the city of Thorold. The list goes on and on, Mr. Speaker.
In the city of Windsor where the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Gray) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) and other member of the government come from, the commissioner of finance was reported recently as admitting that unemployment in the automotive industry was virtually bankrupting the city and saying that the city could no longer afford capital expenditures.
The government has received all these recommendations, Mr. Speaker, yet when the minister and his officials went to Japan they pussyfooted around. The Japanese are good, tough negotiators and they are also good auto manufacturers. This country must take a stand, Mr. Speaker and not be powder-puffed back and forth across the ocean without taking specific action. When negotiations have failed after two and a half years and unemployment is as we see it today, then the government must take unilateral action.
The recommendation being made and followed in virtually every other industrialized nation is that, if need be, the local content of foreign vehicles must be set by legislation. Some may claim that this will increase the cost of the car to the consumer. But that need not be the case if a duty remission is granted. I am not speaking of setting a precedent, Mr. Speaker, because the government already made such an agreement with Volkswagen. A duty remission was given to the German company in return for Canadian content of 85 per cent over a period of four to five years. The only problem with that deal is that Volkswagen has only four per cent of the market in this country. The programs is a good one but it does not mean much in that particular case. It should be applied to the Japanese market as well.
Another approach is to give an incentive to the Japanese to invest in Canada. Oakville, where the Ford Motor Company is situated, is in my constituency of Halton. Tremendous lay-offs and unemployment are being experienced at that plant. As the member for Halton and as a citizen of Oakville, I would not care if a Honda or a Toyota plant were built right next to the Ford plant. As long as Canadians were provided with jobs I would not care. It would help create a healthy economy.
The excuse given by the government is that if it took unilateral action against Japanese imports, then the Japanese would stop buying our natural resources. That is utter hogwash, Mr. Speaker. The Japanese need our natural resources. In fact,
Supply
many are being sold to them already and they will continue to buy them. When the Australians set the 85 per cent local content-and Australia and Canada are the major suppliers of natural resources to Japan-Japan did not reduce its purchases of natural resources by one cent. Neither would it reduce its purchases of natural resources from Canada, so that is not a problem. In fact our natural resources are creating jobs, productivity and a healthy economy in Japan. Then, more often than not, we turn around and buy at inflated prices finished products which were made from our natural resources. There is something wrong. The government is not taking advantage of our natural resources and coming up with incentives for secondary manufacturing in Canada. If we continue to float aimlessly along the lines of the government as far as the economy is concerned, we will no longer have a productive base and we will lose anything we ever had. A typical example is the automotive industry. I believe that Canada cannot affort to lose the automotive industry, just as it cannot afford to lose the shoe industry, the textile industry or any other industry which makes the economic complex work. We are in the process of losing those industries because of lack of action on the part of the government.
The other day in the standing committee the Minister of State for International Trade admitted that the Japanese were not fair traders. They are not fair traders because they have more regulations and controls on imports into Japan than any other country in the world. Perhaps this is why Japan is so successful. I am not suggesting that we regulate our import situation along the same lines as the Japanese have done. If the minister agrees that the Japanese are not fair traders, how can he continue to negotiate with them? Surely he must take some positive action by taking unilateral steps in Parliament to implement legislation which would disallow or slow down the influx of Japanese automobiles into Canada and save jobs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is the second time in less than a week that I have risen in the House to deal with the economic situation in Canada. I am quite pleased to deal with it, because I think it can be done quite positively, while recognizing that the situation as a whole is not altogether ideal. Just before I rose in the House a while ago, 1 read once more the motion moved by the opposition and condemning the government for failing to implement all the policies necessary to support directly the shoe and appliances industry. To make sure that I am well understood, I should like hon. members to read again with me the motion presented by the opposition, because I should like to refer constantly to it in my argument. The motion reads, and I quote:
That this House condemns the government for its chronic failure to implement policies to support the development of a sound industrial sector for Canada, and for the resulting lay-off crisis in every sector of the economy and every region of the country, which has had particularly severe consequences for the auto industry, the resource industry, the energy projects and the producers of consumer goods and appliances.
It is interesting to note that the hon. member's motion seems to suggest that the government has implemented no policy until now and that its failure to act in spite of the economic crisis was the result of a definite political decision on its part. To tease the opposition a little, however, I should like to announce today that the government has selected seven new designated areas for commercial and industrial development under the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board. I am in a position to announce today these new designated areas. They are as follows:	Trois-Rivieres, Cap-de-la-Madeleine,
Grand'Mere, Shawinigan, Drummondville, Victoriaville, Plessisville, Sherbrooke, Magog and Valleyfield in the province of Quebec, as well as Cornwall and Hawkesbury in the province of Ontario. Seven communities designated for industrial renewal.
The interesting thing about the opposition motion is that we are now doing precisely what it asks. We are implementing programs that will provide, not short-term job creation, but long-term job creation based on the processing of our raw materials, the development of our natural resources, in order to
build what the previous speaker spoke of a moment ago, that is, bridges, railroads, highways; in short, to build the country. I am sure all members, including the cabinet and the people of Canada, are agreed on the ideal proposed here, that is, to get our country under construction, to put our people to work. But what is surprising about the other side is that, when we decide to build for the generations to come, the service facilities required to develop the economy, the railroads, the airports, the wharves, which all require additional expenditures, they complain about the deficit. So, on the one hand, they say: Hurry up and bring our economy into the twentieth century, hurry up and invest. On the other hand, they say: do not increase the deficit. Now, if one truly wants to build, not for the next election, but for future generations, one naturally has to borrow because those facilities, those economic tools we are about to build will be useful and practical for a period of one to four generations. Their cost, the cost of that economic infrastructure, that industrial revival must therefore be spread over a period of several years. That obviously explains the deficit. What matters here, which everyone recognizes, is being able to control the deficit, making sure that it is not useless and accumulated merely for the fun of spending public funds. That is what really matters and we all agree. What does cause concern and worry, however, if when opposition parties, strictly for partisan purposes, try to block the programs that are being offered the people merely for the sake of blocking them. Some very substantial amounts of money have been released and are now only starting to be used to help workers.
I come from an area in deep economic trouble. The economy there depends on the iron ore industry, whether in Scheffer-ville, Gagnon, Fermont, Port-Cartier or Sept-lies. The situation there is extremely difficult and, let us make no secret of it, there are people who are experiencing tragedies because of those difficulties. Last week I told the House that even if the government were willing to invest huge amounts of money in those companies for modernization or expansion, it could not put back on the rails industries based on iron ore, on raw material mining, because world markets are scarce, and I refer again to the Iron Ore of Canada, the Sidbec North Mine, the Wabush Mine, and the Quebec Cartier Mining Company. Everybody knows the companies'presidents are not to be blamed for the slack, nor the government, as north shore industries happen to be extremely modern and efficient, and their productivity is fantastic. Telling Canadians they can always rely on the government for solutions is a deceit. It was still worse when the resolution was introduced. The motion now under consideration has been proposed by the Progressive Conservative Party. In the iron ore industry, I had the opportunity to work with the president of the Iron Ore company and I can vouch that none of the plans which could be brought forward could have satisfied that company, not because the company or the workers rejected them, but because world
April 8, 1982

economic conditions were practically impossible. And those are economic and financial facts of the economic market.
Evidently, there are other sectors, which I shall deal with presently, but I wanted to give an example to show that regardless of the means available, you have to wait for an improvement in world conditions. And to pretend the contrary, is literally to deceive people. We are very sensitive. That area on the north shore was one of the first to be designated and the government made considerable grants available to many companies. In Port-Cartier, the ITT company closed when the Progressive Conservative Party was in power but I will not say that party is to be blamed for the closure because it is not so; nor is it on account of us that it is still open. We should be honest in such discussions, but hon. members opposite systematically like to pile it on. Despite the fact that large subsidies were made available to enable other companies to take over the plant, only two were interested. Once again, when the financial analysis is completed, the federal and provincial governments will have to co-operate very closely to ensure the recovery of that mill. Once again it is a matter of supply and demand and whether you belong to the Progressive Conservative, New Democratic or Liberal Party, it is necessary to work with all the economic powers involved. However, you should not suggest that there was no program to restore economic conditions in Port-Cartier or to help mining industries in northern towns-such programs do exist-but you should also admit that politics as well as economics have their limitations. The other side would like us to believe that if they were on this side or we on the other, they could completely change the entire situation. I listened earlier to the hon. member of Joliette (Mr. La Salle) as he lamented the situation, but made no concrete proposals. On the other hand, earlier today, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) gave some examples of concrete ways in which the government is trying to bring about an economic recovery, and more important, to find an approach to industrial renewal.
He talked about Sorel-Tracy, which is included in a designated area along with Sorel in order to give a new impetus to shipbuilding. He talked about Port-Cartier-Sept-Iles for its pulp and paper industry, about Schefferville's ore, as I mentioned a moment ago, about Sydney, Nova Scotia, for its metal primary processing, about Windsor, Ontario for its automotive assembly lines and parts, about Brantford, also in Ontario, for its farm equipment, about Chatham, also in Ontario, for its automotive parts, about L'lslet-Montmagny, for its leisure vehicles and home appliances, about Asbestos, for its mining and about Kitchener-Waterloo for its automotive assembly lines.
Those are not temporary jobs only. With the industrial renewal well under way thanks to incentives and programs designed to update those industries, there will be job opportunities for the young, the old and the natives-for the members who have some in their riding-because it is imperative to find ways of enabling them to develop in society with the same
Supply
advantages others have. I have just given a list of concrete measures and designated areas, but it is impossible to ensure a recovery of this nature in only two or three months' time. A somewhat longer period is needed. It is important to keep those factors in mind when talking about economics. It is argued that nothing is being done. Today, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion made an announcement regarding a factory in Moncton. The department has given a $65,000 grant to help Co-op Atlantic Feed Mill in Moncton update their facilities, thus allowing 47 jobs to be saved. That is a concrete measure. But, of course, it bothers people to hear about concrete situations; it is always more interesting to chase theoretical problems, to try to forget what works and emphasize what does not. That is politically more profitable, and besides, it is quite fair. It is important for the government to show there is another side to the one presented by those opposite.
In St. Quentin, in Quebec, a further amount of $140,000 is provided to promote marketing. This program will permit the creation of new manufacturing and processing facilities. What the country needs is a more modern, efficient economic structure to put more people to work and help the economy. The programs are there and, once again, it is clear in the motion from the opposition that what I have just told you is literally denied. It is clearly indicated, and I quote:
That this House condemn the government for its chronic failure to implement policies to support the development of a sound industrial sector for Canada-
The opposition denies what I have just pointed out. Other elements could say more. The work-sharing program in the Department of Employment and Immigration has been implemented since March 25, 1982, it involves $220 million. The program was announced at the very beginning of the year and by April 2, 1982, 536 applications from companies had been approved, and this will enable 29,292 workers to keep their jobs on a shorter working week basis, and even more important this program prevented 12,805 more workers from being laid-off. Many other applications were sent to the department, and they are being processed.
Twelve thousand people were able to keep their jobs as a result of the implementation of a flexible program under which they can work a shorter week while still getting full pay. This program is interesting because it is optional, which means that you are free to accept it or refuse it. It is also open to discussion which makes consultations and adjustments possible. These are important elements which I should like, as time is running out to compare with what happens in Quebec. Under their present government, Quebecers often complain that governments do not do enough for industry and often blame
16316

April 8, 1982
Supply
the federal government for all their problems. For example la Societe d'amiante du Quebec which is now owned by the Quebec government is neither a private company nor is it run by the federal government. Is it in good shape? Not at all.
This asbestos plant which was bought by the Quebec government has temporarily ceased its operations because of a glut on the market, of stocks piling up and because this material is hard to sell on world markets. However, it is a government-owned company. In Port-Cartier, SIDBEC which is 51 per cent owned by the Quebec government has difficulties finding markets for its products. Yet the federal government has nothing to do with it. The Quebec government in good faith took over a company called Tricofil, which folded up due to the lack of demand. It is a matter of competition. It is a different problem. The fact that a company is owned by the government does not make it necessarily more profitable nor does it open up new markets. The only factor involved is the cost-output ratio in a world situation which should normally be positive. These are significant factors to consider for an understanding of this phenomenon.
Training young people is another factor, as I explained again last week, and the various governments have an obligation to see that training programs are implemented to enable the young people to be really employed, because at the present time, in spite of a 9 per cent unemployment rate in Canada, we are importing labour from abroad. Why? Because we do not have enough skilled workers here. Why? Because, to a large extent, our provincial training programs are not adapted to the labour market. However, it is somewhat ironic that we do have such high unemployment in Canada and that this government has to import labour. Those elements have to be considered within the whole problem. Sure enough, everyone, and we in particular, is suffering from high interest rates. I think that no one would deliberately want to maintain those rates. But ask the experts; there are many differences as to how to set interest rates and at what levels.
Just look at what happened in England or in France, in spite of a so-called socialist government. Unemployment is rising. The value of the French franc has considerably decreased on the exchange market. Of course, if we consider the Canadian problem as such, there seems to be no way out, which is bad enough, but if we compare it with other countries, we see that this problem is less serious and that we have many more alternatives than other countries. And this is the important point. On the other hand, if the government did not do anything, the opposition parties and the people would be justified in demanding programs and more specific job creation programs.
However, we have programs under way and for observers of the political and economic situation, Canada offers very concrete projects that will be implemented shortly, as the opposition is well aware. The opposition is constantly whining. It is as if a surgeon, after making his diagnosis, started to cry over his patient's illness instead of gripping his scalpel firmly to operate. After convalescing, the patient will thank him for
having had the courage to do so. In fact, it takes a lot of courage for this government to implement the measures that we have taken, but we know very well that the health of our country depends on it and that a few months or a few years from now, the people will be very glad that the government showed courage when required. On the other side, they cry over the present sad state of affairs. On this side, we have made a diagnosis and we are trying to find a way of making our country feel better. So, Mr. Speaker, I shall simply conclude by saying that as a parliamentary secretary and a citizen of this country, I share the concern of the opposition parties regarding the economic problems, but we have short-term and long-term measures that will be much more beneficial than all their whining, and I am convinced that we shall continue to build this country in spite of our differences.

Mr. Speaker, I must say I am glad the motion before us today deals with the question of the economy. It says quite categorically that this House condemns the government for its economic policies. Clearly, if there is any time when a government should be condemned for its economic policies, now is the time.
Hear, hear!

Why do I say that, Mr. Speaker? Well, as everyone knows, today the unemployment statistics were issued by Statistics Canada, and for the first time, certainly that I can remember, when we look at the real unemployment statistics which include those people who are discouraged and no longer seeking employment, we now have 1,913,000 unemployed in Canada, almost two million people, and if there is any justification for condemning the government's economic policies, that is it.
In additon, if we look at the unemployment statistics on a regional basis, the unadjusted unemployment rate in every province of Canada has gone up. It is not only the unadjusted rates which have gone up. The province of Newfoundland is one exception in which the seasonally adjusted statistics for unemployment fell by some five tenths of 1 per cent. However, we find that the seasonally adjusted rate still remains at a high of 14.2 per cent in all other regions, from Prince Edward Island to British Columbia. The seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment in this country has gone up. If we look at unemployment by age groups, for example, we find the unadjusted rates for those between the ages of 15 and 24 have gone up, reaching a high today of 18.4 per cent. For those over the age of 25, the unadjusted unemployment rate has gone up to 8 per cent.
If we break down the population in the country on the basis of sex, even these statistics demonstrate that all unemployment rates are going up. For example, with regard to unadjusted unemployment rates for men, the rates have risen from 10 per
April 8, 1982

cent in February to 10.8 per cent in March. For women, the unemployment rates have risen from 9.2 per cent in February to 10 per cent in March.
If we look at the seasonally adjusted statistics on the basis of sex, just to give the government a chance to see whether we are playing with statistics or revealing the social reality, we find that unemployment rates have risen to 9.5 per cent for women and to 8.7 per cent for men.
It is shameful, however you look at it.

If one looks at the statistics today for regions which are hardest hit, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, we find that real unemployment rates-that is, those rates which include people who have given up on the job market and have given up on government policy-range from 21.2 per cent in Quebec to a sky-high rate of 31 per cent in Newfoundland.
The fact is that real unemployment statistics today show that there are two million unemployed people in this country. This is reflected in all regions of the country, in all sub-groups, whether by age or by sex, and in all provinces. This is not a specialized phenomenon. This is not simply a matter of some opposition members playing with statistics. This is a true, tragic reflection of a social reality which, in large part, has been brought about by the insane, insensitive and stupid economic policies of this government.
As a result of the economic statistics which became available today, I took the opportunity to challenge the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in the House with regard to unemployment. I merely wanted to know from him just how high unemployment must go before the government recognizes the folly of its economic policies, changes those economic policies, and seeks to stimulate the economy so as to create jobs for all Canadians. His response was sad. He said that the question was rhetorical. He said, "We are doing everything within our power to assist." He gave specific examples. He mentioned the housing industry in which he claimed that the government was creating 40,000 jobs. He mentioned the use of the unemployment insurance fund, in which he once again claimed an equivalent number of jobs were being created. He mentioned the announcement of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) that the government has created 25,000 to 40,000 jobs. If we are very generous with the government and accept those statistics as face value, we find a total of
120,000	jobs created, in the words of the Minister of Finance, at a time when the statistics clearly show that almost two million people are unemployed in this country. The response of the government is clearly inadequate and weak, and it simply does not meet the needs of Canadians.
The minister went on to say in his response, "We are doing everything possible within the means at our disposal to assist the unemployed in Canada." That was an interesting statement from the Minister of Finance and the chief economic architect of the Liberal government. Why on earth is he able to say, with almost two million people unemployed, that the government is doing all that it can when, using his own response, it has created 120,000 new jobs at the most? Why is he able to say that? Why does he believe that? I am sure that
Supply
the minister is an honest man. I can only conclude that it relates to the way he sees the world and the economy, and his economic philosophy. I think that that economic philosophy was quite readily reflected in recent statements by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Bouey. In the issue of The Globe and Mail dated April 7, 1982, Mr. Bouey's sentiments were expressed. The article quoted Mr. Bouey as saying that Canadians must be prepared to take a cut in living standards to combat unemployment, inflation and recession. Yesterday, Bank of Canada Governor Gerald Bouey said:
I am sometimes asked . . . how high does the rate of unemployment have to go, how many foreclosures have to occur, before the bank will give up its policy of monetary restraint.
His response was very much like the response given to me by the Minister of Finance. They will stick by their economic theories and philosophies. They refuse to do anything to help Canadian people when they need help and jobs. Why? It is because of the central economic philosophy, and the governor is quoted quite clearly in The Globe and Mail. In fact, he is quoted as having listed the following to be detriments to the creation of employment: government regulation, marketing boards and the minimum wage. He quotes these as being antimarket culprits. Therefore, what he is really saying is that he is a believer in the unregulated market and believes that the unregulated market will somehow create wealth and jobs for Canadians. That is clearly not working today. These are not the times for believers in economic theory. These are not the times for the Friedmans and Reaganites of the world, the people who, through some unexamined belief in an economic theory, continue to steer the ship of state into troubled waters and to abandon Canadians without care. They are operating on the basis of a belief in an economic theory rather than on the basis of social reality.
If only they would look at what is happening in the economy, if only they would look at what is happening to people and if only they would read the statistics produced by their own government departments which demonstrate the fact that unheard numbers of people are unemployed today, they would find that a change in economic policy is required in order to get those people back to work. They must re-examine their belief and take some pragmatic, caring action in order to meet the needs of Canadians. However, instead of a rational, humane, objective, openminded look at economic matters, what we get from this government is not only statements of philosophical commitment from the Minister of Finance, but the public relations exercises of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) as well. He has now become the front man for this Liberal government. What has he done as the front man? Quite simply, he goes around setting up smokescreens and he does this by holding press conferences every couple of weeks in which he announces some new "job creation" measures.

He announces them every time.

April 8, 1982
Supply

And he goes on reshuffling existing funds. When we look closely at some of the announcements we find this. In one he has said there will be a $200 million effort. That was $200 million for job creation. When we look closely, what we find is that there is only $20 million in there which had to do with direct job creation, one tenth of the figure announced.
A couple of weeks later, he made another $200 million announcement with regard to mining and forestry. When we examined that closely, we found there was only some 50 million new dollars in that package over a two-year period. These are inflated announcements. They are attempts by the government to set up a smokescreen behind which it can hide so that it does not have to face the economic realities which ordinary Canadians have to face in their day to day lives.
But this is not the end of these public relations gimmicks. Yesterday the Minister of Employment and Immigration held a national conference on work-sharing in which he was expressing his enthusiasm and his feelings that work-sharing was a success. That is like saying that unemployment insurance is a success because there are so many people on it. The fact that people need help is a demonstration of the failure of the economic policies of the government, and not of their success.
Hear, hear!

The work-sharing, using the minister's own figures, has been able to help 13,600 people to retain their jobs. Well, I am sure that for those 13,600 individuals that is a welcome measure, but for the other real, though not official, two million Canadians who remain unemployed, it is a pitiful response, inadequate and insensitive. It is simply a public relations gesture, it is not an economic response, it is not a compassionate response; it is an attempt to use the media to protect the government from the anger of Canadians at a time when that anger is justified.
Right on.

While we have the Minister of Finance making his philosophical statements and the minister of employment engaging in his public relations exercises, what is going on in the economy, what is happening in Canada? Well, if we look at it closely, Mr. Speaker, we can see quite clearly what is happening. I am going to quote from some objective sources. I will quote from The Globe and Mail of Tuesday, April 6, 1982. The picture that we find is that Canada is suffering from the worst economic crisis since 1947. The Conference Board of Canada recently did a survey of the findings of economic forecasters. I quote from The Globe and Mail.
Canada is gripped by what is probably the worst recession since 1947 and unemployment will remain at near record levels for the rest of the year, according to a survey of 18 economic forecasters.
The report in The Globe and Mail goes on to say:
The Conference Board of Canada survey found most forecasters much more pessimistic about 1982's economic rate and unemployment prospects than they were last fall yet no more hopeful about the chances for bringing down inflation.
The significance of that last phrase is that every action by this government is justified in the name of fighting inflation. Clearly, inflation is not going down, their policies are not working, so why do they not re-examine them and why do they not consider the people who need work now?
It is not only the Conference Board of Canada that draws this picture of the economy for us. We go to a government agency, Statistics Canada. They indicate quite clearly that there is no end in sight to the recession in the following statement:
There is still no end in sight for the current economic recession, according to the government's chief statistical agency. In fact, the few indicators that surfaced in last month's report suggesting that the economy might improve have practically vanished.
I go on to some solutions they suggest:
One way the government could pull the economy out of the recession is by lowering the value of the dollar hence making exports more competitive on the world markets.
A little further on, report says:
The Bank of Canada has warned that it will not relent on its tight money policy, that it will not allow the dollar to decline, it has pushed up its lending rate slightly to 15.40 per cent from 15.32 per cent.
They are not willing to accept or consider changes in policy but they are willing to push up the interest rates and thereby up the inflation rate and thereby put more people on the unemployment rolls.
It is not just the members of this party here who are drawing a gloomy picture of the economy. It is objective agencies of the government and the community who point out that we are in an economic crisis. But is this economic crisis one that is as the Minister of Finance described it, an international crisis under which we have no influence or no control? Must it always be and is it an act of God? Is it an act of fate? Is it an historical inevitability? Must we continue in this sea of troubles with no hope for relief?
We probably must, if we share the economic philosophy of the government, if we believe, as the government seems to believe, in an unregulated free market economy.
I believe somewhat differently, Mr. Speaker. I believe in a mixed economy but I also believe that the government can take hold of the economy, can make the economy serve the needs of the people and can provide employment. That is not only a philosophical position that I take in saying that, it is also a philosophical posture that can be translated into practical proposals.
I want to refer to a comprehensive proposal that was made by the leader of our party recently, which is described as "a new employment option for Canada". There are five parts to it. Quite simply, it is a practical, humane suggestion to the government as to how we can get the economy moving again and get Canadians back to work. I will describe it fairly briefly and quickly, but I would like to get the essence of it across to the government so that it can realize that it is possible to do something about the economy and to do something now.
The first point focuses upon the domestic Canadian economy and really says that what we have to do in Canada is be
April 8, 1982

willing to negotiate production agreements in key economic sectors such as machinery and transportation. We have to negotiate production agreements with multinational corporations. We have to say, "okay, if you want a piece of our market"-and that is why they are here, they want a piece of our market-"then you have to do a fair share of the manufacturing in Canada, you have to provide Canada with a fair share of the jobs."
That would be a good start.

If they are not willing to do that, then we have to be willing to use some lever in order to convince them that we are serious in these negotiations, that we are prepared to look at measures such as emergency surcharges, look at measures including subsidies and various kinds of tax measures in order to convince the multinationals that we are serious about providing employment for Canada and that when we enter into negotiations for jobs for Canadians, we mean it.
And make them for the autoworkers.

Exactly. The second point of this New Employment Option relates to the export market and it points out that countries like France and West Germany provide all sorts of assistance for their export industries and that we need to do a similar kind of thing here in Canada. We have to underwrite the risks faced by our exporters and, we have to provide a comprehensive coverage of production, credit, accident, commercial, exchange rate, inflation and market development risks. In other words, we have to use the government to put our export industries on a competitive footing with the rest of the industrial world. The third point in this new employment option relates to tax cuts. We want to provide an immediate tax cut for low and middle-income Canadians.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I understand that the hon. member may wish to continue, but his time has expired. I would have to seek, on his behalf, the unanimous consent of the House to permit him to continue for a moment or two. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will wind up very quickly. The third measure in this employment package relates to tax cuts. The fourth measure relates to housing. The fifth relates to interest rates. I will not go into the details of these measures now because my time has run out.
Quite simply, I wanted to point out that rather than adopting these sort of practical proposals and putting them into action, what is happening in Canada is that more and more Canadians are on the welfare rolls. In fact, today there have been estimates that 250,000 of those Canadians on the welfare rolls are, in fact, employable Canadians. What we have in Canada today is a policy of putting workers on welfare. What we need is a policy for putting workers back to work. We must get the government to start working on the economy so
Supply
Canadians can get back to work and earn a decent living. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, it was very interesting listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) speaking on the economy and what government must do in order to create conditions for a fast growing and highly productive economy. However, I think the hon. member must realize, as all of us must to a great extent, that this does not depend entirely on the government. The government cannot make the economy work by snapping its fingers or by saying that it should work. It requires co-operation from all the players in the economic system. It takes cooperation from labour, from the business community and it certainly takes co-operation from governments.
In some cases in the past, government policies at the federal and provincial level have not been as effective as we would have liked them to be in promoting growth and development. Governments have recognized that fact and have attempted to modify policies in order to try to improve them.
For example, the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Roberts) indicated earlier that we realize that research and development in Canada is below what we would like to see it, below what other nations have achieved and below where we think it should be. Indeed, the government has brought forward policies to try to improve the situation and increase the amount of research and development. There have been many initiatives taken recently to try to improve research and development.
Since I am from Ottawa I know for a fact that those policies are in place and have been of assistance and are, indeed, creating an environment in which research and development can grow much faster than it has in the past. Although we do not necessarily like the term, people from outside of Ottawa have called it "silicone valley north", referring to the Ottawa Valley with its high technology industry which has grown from virtually nothing. It started out of the Bell Northern research labs and the Bell Canada research labs which were located here. People who worked in those labs spun out of that industry and developed their own companies like Mitel, Gandalf, Nabu and other companies.
What about the west?
